```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse=TRUE, comment="#>", fig.width=7, fig.height=4)
library(AdaReFun)
```

AdaReFun fits **scalar-on-function** regression: each row is a sampled curve,
and each curve has one scalar response. It is not a function-on-scalar or
function-on-function fitting interface.

## A small, reproducible demonstration

This artificial dataset illustrates the interface, not the paper's performance
claims. The training/validation split is explicit. No test set is used for
selection. The modest tuning grids keep this example short.

```{r data}
set.seed(2026)
t <- seq(0, 1, length.out=51)
n <- 60
scores <- matrix(rnorm(n*6), n, 6)
x <- scores %*% t(sapply(1:6, function(j) sin(j*pi*t)))
beta <- ifelse(t >= .35 & t <= .65, 0, 1.5*sin(2*pi*t))
w <- c(.01, rep(.02,49), .01)
y <- .5 + drop(x %*% (w*beta)) + rnorm(n, sd=.15)
```

`x` is an observations-by-grid matrix. `t` contains argument locations on
`[0,1]`; `beta` is the demonstration truth. The vector `w` is a trapezoidal
integration rule used only to generate the synthetic response.

```{r fit}
selection <- arfc_select(y[1:40], x[1:40,], t,
  validation=list(y=y[41:60], x=x[41:60,]),
  lambda=c(1e-4, 1e-3, 1e-2), kappa=c(1e-5, 1e-4),
  levels=c(4L,8L,16L))
selection$selection
```

## Inspect the choice and its coefficient

```{r validation}
plot(selection, type="validation")
```

```{r coefficient}
plot(selection, type="coefficient")
```

`arfc_select()` returns one training-fitted model. It neither averages the four
candidates nor silently refits on the validation observations. For a stated
resolution and penalty, use `arfc()` directly. Predictions use the training
centering quantities:

```{r prediction}
head(predict(selection, x[41:60,]))
```

Read the method guide before interpreting exact zeros as structural evidence.
Finite-precision cutoff/refit conventions and convergence diagnostics matter.
